body:
Silicon Valley venture capital giant Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) is hitting the ground in South Korea to seek out AI hardware and infrastructure companies. Just one month after raising an $1.1 billion (approximately ₩1.5 trillion) AI infrastructure-focused fund, the firm's investment chief is visiting South Korea to explore partnership possibilities with local companies.

According to a16z on the 12th, Raghu Raghuram, managing partner and general partner, is visiting South Korea with the infrastructure investment team. He oversees investments across the full spectrum of AI infrastructure at a16z, from software to hardware, and leads global strategy for growth-stage portfolio companies. Before joining a16z, he held key product and management roles at global cloud infrastructure company VMware for approximately 20 years.

This visit marks the first major initiative since the launch of the "Machine Age Fund" in September. The fund targets core hardware including semiconductors, computing, memory, and networking, as well as foundational technologies essential for AI infrastructure buildout such as power, cooling, and data centers. a16z plans to concentrate investments in emerging companies with the potential to build differentiated competitive advantages.

During the visit, Raghuram and the investment team will meet with key companies and stakeholders in South Korea's AI hardware and infrastructure sector to discuss technology development and commercialization opportunities, and explore partnership possibilities with a16z portfolio companies. They will also discuss ways to support the creation of new AI-based businesses and the growth of South Korean companies.

Focus on Semiconductors and Robotics

a16z has identified semiconductors and robotics as the primary areas for collaboration with South Korea. The firm believes that South Korea's strengths in semiconductors, memory, and advanced manufacturing create diverse collaboration opportunities in AI hardware and computing infrastructure. Robotics is also viewed as a key collaboration area as AI technology adoption continues to expand.

"AI's advancement is rapidly transforming not just software but the entire technology infrastructure stack," said Raghuram. "South Korea possesses world-class technology capabilities and a robust industrial base in critical areas such as semiconductors and robotics, and I look forward to meeting directly with South Korean companies and industry stakeholders during this visit to broadly discuss new technologies and business opportunities."

An Extension of Expanding South Korea Presence

This visit signals that a16z's approach to the South Korean market is becoming increasingly concrete. In late 2025, a16z hired Park Sung-mo as head of Asia-Pacific (APAC) go-to-market, its first hire in South Korea, to pursue collaboration with the domestic crypto ecosystem. The firm has recently expanded its engagement and partnership efforts across South Korea's technology industry, including AI, and Raghuram's visit represents a continuation of that trajectory.

The fund is based on a16z's assessment that AI's advancement is rapidly transforming the entire technology infrastructure landscape beyond software. As computing resources, memory bandwidth, power supply, and thermal management required for large-scale AI model training and inference emerge as bottlenecks, investment demand is growing for emerging companies with differentiated technologies in these areas.

Implications from an Investor Perspective

A global VC directly seeking out South Korean companies demonstrates that South Korea's AI hardware ecosystem is being recognized by global investors as an attractive collaboration target. In particular, the manufacturing capabilities and technological expertise that South Korean companies possess in semiconductors and memory are essential components for AI infrastructure buildout.

However, a16z has not announced any specific investment deals or amounts during this visit. Given that exploring partnership possibilities and discussing technology and business opportunities are the priorities, additional review processes are expected before any actual investments or collaborations materialize. Whether specific collaboration cases emerge between a16z portfolio companies and South Korean firms, and whether a portion of the Machine Age Fund's capital will be allocated to South Korean companies, remain key points of interest.
